strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in decentralized foundation model adaptation: balancing personalization and out-of-distribution generalization in vision-language models (VLMs).
The proposed method of decoupling the multi-modal adapter into local modality-specific projections and a globally aggregated cross-modal projection is intuitive and communication-efficient.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide suite of tasks, including base-to-novel generalization, domain shift (DomainNet, Office-Caltech10), and label shift (CIFAR-10/100), showing consistent improvements in generalization over several federated prompt tuning baselines.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The multi-modal adapter architecture is largely borrowed directly from prior work (MMA, Yang et al., CVPR 2024), and the federated optimization scheme is a straightforward parameter-split personalization strategy (analogous to FedPer/FedRep applied to adapter sub-matrices).

Missing adapter-based federated baselines: The comparison is conducted almost exclusively against federated prompt learning methods (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP). To substantiate the claim that the proposed asymmetric multi-modal adapter is responsible for the gains, the paper should include adapter-based FL baselines (e.g., FedAvg with uni-modal CLIP-Adapter/LoRA, fully federated MMA without personalization, and fully local adapters).

Lack of ablation studies in the main text: The paper does not provide ablation studies analyzing critical design choices, such as which adapter components should be shared vs. kept local (e.g., sharing up/down projections instead of the cross-modal projection), the effect of the insertion block depth $\ell$, or the impact of bottleneck dimension $r$ and scaling factor $\alpha$.

Minor inconsistencies and omissions: The abstract mentions eleven datasets, Section 5.1 introduces nine datasets (listing six visual classification datasets), yet Table 1 reports results on seven datasets (including OxfordPets, which was omitted from the list in Section 5.1). Furthermore, the exact value of starting layer $\ell$ is not specified in the main experimental setup.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: achieving a good balance between personalization and out-of-distribution/novel class generalization for Vision-Language Models in federated learning.

The proposed asymmetric optimization scheme—keeping modality-specific projections local while communicating and aggregating the shared cross-modal projection—is intuitive, conceptually clean, and communication-efficient.

Extensive empirical evaluations across a wide range of benchmarks (7 fine-grained classification datasets, DomainNet, Office-Caltech10, and CIFAR-10/100) under different heterogeneity setups (pathological label shift, Dirichlet label shift, and domain shift).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The multi-modal adapter architecture is directly adopted from existing work (MMA, Yang et al., CVPR 2024), and the federated optimization relies on a standard parameter-decoupled split (similar to FedPer/PartialFed) where some layers are local and others are globally averaged.

Unfair/incomplete baseline comparison: All federated learning baselines evaluated (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP) are prompt-tuning methods. It remains unclear whether the performance gains stem from the proposed federated aggregation scheme or simply from adapters being inherently more expressive/effective than prompt tuning. Comparisons with adapter-based FL methods (e.g., federated LoRA, federated Tip-Adapter, or standard FedAvg on MMA) are missing.

Lack of ablation studies: The paper does not provide ablations on key design choices. For instance, what happens if all adapter parameters are aggregated via FedAvg, or if only the modality-specific projections are shared while the cross-modal projection is kept local? What is the impact of varying the bottleneck dimension $r$ or adapter insertion depth $\ell$?

Minor inconsistencies and missing appendix: On page 9, DomainNet has 12 clients and Office-Caltech10 has 8 clients, but on page 11, the text contradicts this by stating '8 clients for DomainNet and 12 clients for Office-Caltech10'. Furthermore, multiple references are made to supplementary details in an appendix, but no appendix is included in the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely topic: extending parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for large vision-language models (VLMs) into personalized federated learning (PFL).

The empirical evaluation spans multiple benchmarks, covering base-to-novel generalization, label skew, and feature/domain shifts across several standard datasets (SUN397, Flowers102, DomainNet, CIFAR, etc.).
The overall writing and structure are generally clear and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The adapter architecture is adopted directly from prior centralized work (MMA [38]), and the federated optimization is a direct application of standard FedAvg to the shared middle projection matrix while keeping the up/down projection matrices local (analogous to classic parameter-split approaches like FedPer/FedRep). The paper lacks significant algorithmic or theoretical innovation tailored to multi-modal federated learning.

Lack of essential adapter-based baselines: All federated baselines compared in the paper (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP) are prompt-tuning methods. There are no adapter-based federated baselines, such as FedAvg applied to the full MMA adapter, FedAvg with unimodal adapters (e.g., CLIP-Adapter), or standard FedPer applied to adapters/LoRA. Consequently, it is unclear whether performance improvements arise from the proposed asymmetric sharing scheme or simply from the higher expressive capacity of multi-modal adapters over prompt tuning.

Missing ablation studies: The paper provides no ablations to substantiate its core architectural choices. Crucial questions remain unanswered, such as: (1) What is the performance if all adapter parameters are averaged vs. fully local vs. the proposed split? (2) What happens if the down/up projections are shared while the middle projection is local? (3) How sensitive is the method to the insertion layer depth $\ell$, bottleneck dimension $r$, and scaling factor $\alpha$?

Soundness concern regarding feature space alignment: Clients learn local, unconstrained down-projection matrices $W_{jd,i}$, meaning that the intermediate representations fed into the shared projection $W_{js}$ lie in client-specific, non-aligned coordinate spaces. Averaging $W_{js}$ globally across clients when its input and output spaces are governed by disparate local linear transformations creates representational inconsistency, which the paper neither analyzes nor addresses.

Minor inconsistencies and presentation issues: Section 5.1 contains typos (e.g., 'Implimentation Details', duplicate 'with with'). Furthermore, the text on page 9 states $N = 12$ for DomainNet and $N = 8$ for Office-Caltech10, whereas Section 5.2 on page 11 reverses these numbers ('8 clients for DomainNet and 12 clients for Office-Caltech10').

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing a timely and relevant problem: balancing personalization and generalization (base-to-novel and domain shift) in personalized federated fine-tuning of vision-language models (VLMs).

Clean, elegant, and communication-efficient design: by decoupling the multi-modal adapter into local modality-specific up/down-projections and a globally shared cross-modal projection, the framework achieves high communication efficiency (only transmitting the low-rank shared projection, e.g., 3,072 parameters per round).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 11 benchmark datasets covering base-to-novel generalization, pathological label skews, Dirichlet partitions (CIFAR-10/100), and feature/domain shifts (DomainNet and Office-Caltech10).
Extensive ablation studies and efficiency analyses (computation, training time, GPU memory, scaling factors, adapter bottleneck dimensions, starting layer, and sharing strategies).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the multi-modal adapter (MMA) architecture is adopted from Yang et al. (CVPR 2024), and the federated split learning strategy (sharing certain layers while keeping others local) is a classic paradigm in personalized federated learning (e.g., FedPer, FedRep).

Discrepancy in local trainable parameter budget across baselines: pFedMMA utilizes ~248k trainable parameters per client compared to 8k–16k in prompt-based baselines (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP). Although pFedMMA transmits fewer parameters per round, comparing against standard unimodal federated adapter or LoRA baselines would help isolate whether the performance gains stem from the multi-modal adapter structure or parameter capacity alone.
Minor presentation and typographical errors, such as 'Implimentation Details' on page 7 and 'lable shift' in the captions of Table 3 and Table 9/10.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the critical trade-off between personalization and out-of-distribution/novel class generalization in personalized federated learning with vision-language models.

The proposed pFedMMA framework presents an elegant and communication-efficient design: by keeping modality-specific up- and down-projections local and only communicating the compact cross-modal shared projection (r x r), communication overhead is drastically reduced (only ~3,072 parameters per round).

Extensive empirical evaluation covering 11 diverse datasets across multiple challenging scenarios, including few-shot base-to-novel generalization, pathological label skews, Dirichlet label skews, and domain/feature shifts (DomainNet and Office-Caltech10).

Thorough ablation studies and cost analysis, investigating adapter dimensions, scaling factors, layer placement, parameter sharing strategies, training time, memory consumption, and multiple model backbones (ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32).
weaknesses: The core architectural component is directly adopted from existing centralized multi-modal adapters (Yang et al., CVPR 2024), and the federated strategy follows the well-established paradigm of partial parameter personalization (sharing middle representations while keeping input/output projections local). Hence, the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental.

Comparisons are restricted almost entirely to prompt-tuning baselines (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP). Given that pFedMMA uses adapter modules with significantly more local trainable parameters (~248k vs. 8k–74k for prompt methods, as shown in Table 17), it remains unclear whether the performance gains stem from the multi-modal adapter structure itself or simply the higher capacity and expressiveness of adapter-based tuning compared to text prompt tuning. Including federated LoRA or federated unimodal adapter baselines would make the evaluation much more convincing.

There are unexplained anomalies in the multi-domain results: in Table 10, pFedMMA reports 0.00% accuracy on specific domains (e.g., DomainNet Painting under beta=0.5 with one domain per client, and DomainNet Real under beta=0.1). The manuscript does not discuss why these extreme failures occur.

Minor presentation flaws and typos throughout the manuscript, such as 'Implimentation Details' on page 7, 'lable shift' in the captions of Table 3 and Table 10, and indexing notation inconsistencies in Algorithm 1 line 14 (where client index i is listed as belonging to {l, ..., L}).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: the trade-off between personalization and base-to-novel generalization in federated fine-tuning of vision-language models.

The experimental evaluation is extensive across 11 datasets, encompassing base-to-novel class generalization, varying few-shot settings (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 shots), Dirichlet label heterogeneity, and domain shift scenarios on DomainNet and Office-Caltech10.

Comprehensive ablations and cost analyses are provided in the paper and appendix, detailing communication cost, parameter efficiency, training time, adapter bottleneck dimensions, scaling factor, and layer placement.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The multi-modal adapter structure is adopted directly from existing centralized work (Yang et al., CVPR 2024), and the federated strategy simply applies standard FedAvg to the middle projection matrix ($W_s$) while keeping the up/down projections local.

Lack of adapter-based and LoRA federated baselines: All empirical comparisons are made against prompt-tuning methods (PromptFL, FedPGP, FedOTP, pFedMoAP). It remains unclear whether the reported performance gains stem from the proposed federated multi-modal adapter scheme or simply from adapters having inherently higher expressive capacity/trainable parameters compared to prompt tuning. Comparisons with federated LoRA or unimodal adapters (e.g., AdaptFormer or CLIP-Adapter with local/global splits) are missing.

Potential feature space misalignment for the shared component: The middle layer $W_s$ is aggregated globally via FedAvg, but the preceding down-projections $W_d$ are completely unconstrained and updated locally per client. Without explicit alignment or regularization, client-specific coordinate rotations can cause the input representations entering $W_s$ to drift, making standard parameter averaging mathematically problematic and poorly motivated.
Minor presentation flaws: Noticeable typos exist in section headings and table captions (e.g., 'Implimentation Details' on page 7, 'lable shift' in the caption of Table 3 and Table 9).
